name: Germanic Languages

formality.description: Most Germanic languages have T-V pronominal distinctions: German du/Sie, Dutch je(jij)/u, Swedish du/ni (historically, now largely replaced by du-reform), Norwegian du/De (archaic). English is the major exception, having lost its T-V distinction (thou/you → universal you). Icelandic also lacks a formal pronoun. Default to formal (V) in professional contexts for languages that retain it.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Germanic languages have grammatical gender, but systems vary: German, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål have masculine/feminine/neuter. Dutch and Swedish have common/neuter (two genders). Danish has common/neuter. English has lost grammatical gender almost entirely (retained only in pronouns). Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, and pronouns.

linguisticChallenges.compoundWordFormation: Germanic languages (especially German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Icelandic) form compound nouns by concatenation without spaces: German Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaft. Compound splitting for translation and compound generation in the target are both error-prone. English uses spaces in compounds, while other Germanic languages do not.
linguisticChallenges.separablePrefixVerbs: German and Dutch have separable prefix verbs (German: anfangen → ich fange an; Dutch: opbellen → ik bel op) where the prefix detaches and moves to the end of the clause. This creates long-distance dependencies that MT systems must track across clause boundaries.
linguisticChallenges.v2WordOrder: Most Germanic languages (German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish) follow V2 (verb-second) word order in main clauses — the finite verb must be the second constituent regardless of what fills first position. Subordinate clauses have verb-final order (German, Dutch). This systematic word order alternation is a consistent source of MT errors.
linguisticChallenges.articleSystem: Germanic languages have both definite and indefinite articles, but their realization varies: Scandinavian languages suffix the definite article (Swedish hus-et 'the house'), while German/Dutch/English use freestanding articles. The double definiteness of Scandinavian (both suffix and freestanding article with adjectives) is a further complexity.
linguisticChallenges.caseVestiges: Full case systems survive in German (4 cases) and Icelandic (4 cases). Other Germanic languages have reduced case to pronouns only (English I/me, Swedish jag/mig) or lost it almost entirely (Dutch, Danish). German case interacts with gender and number to create complex declension tables.
linguisticChallenges.modalParticles: German and Dutch make extensive use of modal particles (doch, mal, ja, schon, eben; toch, maar, wel, even) that add nuance, emphasis, or pragmatic force to sentences. These particles have no direct equivalents in most other languages and are frequently dropped or mistranslated by MT.

notes: Genus card for Germanic languages (English, German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Icelandic, Afrikaans, Yiddish, etc.). All use Latin script. T-V formality applies to most members but not English or Icelandic. Gender system varies from 3-gender (German) to 2-gender (Dutch, Swedish) to none (English).

regions.region: Britain, Germany, Netherlands, Scandinavia, Iceland, global (English diaspora), South Africa (Afrikaans)
